item.description:
I was 13, sitting in a barbershop in Amman with my younger brother, transfixed by what we were witnessing on the television, when the men around us began to chant “Allahu Akbar.” It took a moment for a dozen grown men to realize what they were watching: a victory for Islam and our people. As the towers fell, as the Pentagon burned, as the civilized world reacted in horror, we rejoiced — America, the Great Satan, had fallen. Since then I have heard “Allahu Akbar” again and again — from men beheading captives in Iraq, from those who burned people alive in cages in Syria, from suicide bombers who walked into Israeli and Parisian cafés, and in gay bars and synagogues in America when terrorists opened fire on innocence. item.title: How Donald Trump boxed his party in
item.description:
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. When Donald Trump looks at a map, he doesn’t see nations. He sees property. All of those pretty colors do not represent actual places filled with human beings who have distinct cultures, languages, and histories; the planet, to Trump, is a big board game, like Risk or Monopoly. Greenland isn’t a real location—it’s a valuable chunk of territory nestled between Boardwalk and Park Place. The Strait of Hormuz isn’t an international waterway—it’s a thing to control somewhere between Kamchatka and East Africa. item.title: New York, 25 Years Later
item.description:
Photographs by Sasha Arutyunova L ike most New Englanders of a certain generation, my parents viewed New York City with distrust. They associated their neighbor to the south with “The Bronx Is Burning,” Bernhard Goetz, blackouts, bankruptcy, and the famous New York Daily News headline Ford to City: Drop Dead . The heart of Manhattan was a decadent playground for the wealthy, while outlying neighborhoods were plagued by desperate poverty and violence. I grew up only 200 miles away, and yet my parents never took me there as a kid. But if New York felt menacing and foreign to them, in reality, it is the most American of cities. New York is a symbol of the nation’s money and power, its diversity and freedom. It is our capital of culture, a proudly loud and bustling melting pot. And for those who wanted to humble the world’s sole superpower, New York was the perfect place to strike 25 years…
